Peevish means being easily annoyed and irritated — especially by small, trivial things — in a childish, sulky, or whiny way.

When you call someone peevish, you are saying two things at once: they are in an irritated, grumpy mood and that irritation seems petty, unreasonable, or out of proportion to what caused it.

Think of a tired child who has not had a nap. Nothing is seriously wrong, but every tiny thing bothers them. They complain constantly. They snap at people. They are not furious — they are just grumpy, sulky, and difficult. That is peevish behavior.

A peevish person:

  • Gets annoyed easily and quickly
  • Complains in a whiny, fretful way
  • Makes a fuss over things that most people would brush off
  • Comes across as childish or unnecessarily difficult

The key idea is the pettiness of it. Big, justified anger is not peevish. Peevish is the low-level, simmering, whiny kind of irritability — the kind that makes other people roll their eyes a little.
What Makes "Peevish" Special (The Tone It Carries)

This is important: when you describe someone as peevish, you are being slightly dismissive of their complaints. You are quietly suggesting that they are overreacting, that their grievances are not entirely valid, or that they are behaving immaturely.

It is not a neutral word. It carries a subtle judgment — almost like saying, "Stop being difficult over nothing."

So if someone calls you peevish, they are not just saying you are annoyed — they are saying your annoyance seems unreasonable and a bit childish.

These words all live in the same neighborhood, but they are not the same:

Peevish vs. Irritable — "Irritable" simply means easily annoyed. "Peevish" adds the layer of pettiness and childishness. A peevish person is irritable in a whiny, trivial way.

Peevish vs. Grumpy — "Grumpy" is a general, low mood — quiet and sullen. A peevish person is more actively complaining and fussing. Peevish is grumpy with a whine attached to it.

Peevish vs. Sulky — "Sulky" suggests someone who has gone quiet, withdrawn, and moody. Peevish people are not quiet — they are complaining and showing their irritation outwardly.

Peevish vs. Cross — "Cross" just means angry or annoyed. "Peevish" is more specific: it is a particular flavor of annoyance that feels petty and small.

Peevish vs. Cantankerous — "Cantankerous" describes someone who is argumentative, stubborn, and combative. It is stronger and more aggressive. Peevish is softer — more of a whine than a fight.
Can It Describe Both a Moment and a Personality?

Yes — and this is useful to know.

Temporary state: Someone can feel or seem peevish in a particular moment — perhaps because they are tired, hungry, or frustrated.

"She was peevish all morning because her flight had been delayed."

Personality trait: Someone can also be a peevish person by nature — meaning they are generally prone to this kind of irritable, fussy behavior as part of their character.

"He was a peevish old man who complained about everything."

• "The peevish customer complained that his soup was a degree too cold." (petty, trivial complaint)
  • "Don't be so peevish — missing the bus is not the end of the world." (dismissing someone's overreaction)
  • "After a long day without food, she became peevish and snapped at her friends." (temporary state)
  • "His peevish remarks about the décor annoyed everyone at the party." (whiny, unnecessary criticism)
  • "The child's peevish whining made it impossible to have a calm conversation." (childish irritability)
The Single Sentence to Remember It Forever

Peevish = irritable and complaining in a petty, childish way — over things that are too small to deserve such a fuss.

If you can picture a sulky child making a scene because their biscuit broke in half — that is the spirit of peevish, perfectly captured.
